av_event.line_text: Callum: Yeah. Rubbish at it. Rushed the last two cos I got bored.
av_event.what: An elderly cat jumps up onto the kitchen worktop behind Carys, walks slowly past the kettle and bread bin, then drops down out of frame; Carys does not turn round.

text:
A: Hello. Can you hear me all right?
B: Yeah, fine. You alright?
A: Fine, thanks. I'm Carys.
B: Callum.
A: Right. Erm, so I suppose we just chat. What do you do, Callum?
B: Student. Computer science at Wolverhampton, second year. Do the odd Saturday at a tyre place when I'm skint.
A: Oh, okay. And do you enjoy it? The course, I mean, not the tyres.
B: Bits of it. The coding's alright, getting stuff to actually run. The theory and the write-ups I could do without, to be honest. Half the modules feel like they're just there to fill the timetable, do you know what I mean.
A: Yeah, I remember some of those. Mine was civil engineering, a long time ago now.
B: That what you do then?
A: It is, yeah. I'm a civil engineer at a consultancy, I do flood risk and drainage mostly. So, councils across North Wales and Cheshire come to us with, erm, say an estate that floods every winter, or a culvert that can't cope, and I model how the water moves and work out what we can actually do about it.
B: Like the floods you see on the news, people in canoes down the high street.
A: Sort of, yeah. Hopefully I'm the reason you don't see it on the news. That's the idea, anyway.
B: Fair. Sounds more useful than half of what I do.
A: Well, someone's got to write the software for the models, to be fair. Did you do the puzzle at the start?
B: Yeah. Rubbish at it. Rushed the last two cos I got bored.
A: I quite liked it, actually. I do the Saturday cryptic, so I'm used to staring at things until they give in.
B: Cryptic crosswords. My nan does them. Well, she does the easy ones.
A: There's no shame in the easy ones. So what are you thinking of doing after? Have you got a placement year?
B: Nah. Not yet. My tutor keeps on at me about it. Something'll turn up.
A: Hm. That's exactly what my son says about his mocks.
B: How old's he?
A: Sixteen. He's very relaxed about it. Unlike me.
B: Sounds about right, yeah.
A: I'll be honest with you though, I mentor graduates at work, and the ones who got placements sorted early had a much easier time. I'm not nagging. Well, I am a bit.
B: No, you're probably right, I know I'm leaving it late. I just can't get myself bothered till it's urgent. Did two years on nights in a warehouse before uni, so I'm not exactly panicking, if that makes sense. Anything's better than nights.
A: That makes sense, yeah. My dad was at the steelworks, so I understand wanting something steady.
B: Yeah. That's it really.
A: Is that a Wolves scarf behind you?
B: Yeah, through my dad. Watch most of them down the pub. You into football?
A: Not really. Rugby, for the Six Nations. My son and I watch Wales and I get more worked up than I should.
B: Never got rugby, mate. Too many stoppages.
A: Yeah, no, I've heard that one before.
